newsitem.title: UK: German banker attacks France for EMU budget move.
newsitem.headline: German banker attacks France for EMU budget move.

text.p: A member of Germany's powerful central bank, the Bundesbank, criticised France on Tuesday for jeopardising the success of the European Union's planned single currency by resorting to creative accounting in its budget.

Raimut Jochimsen, a member of the Bundesbank's governing central council, told BBC television that France had sent a wrong signal to other countries by transferring $7.2 billion from state-owned France Telecom to its national budget.

Jochimsen said that the German public would not accept a single currency, due to be launched on January 1, 1999, based on a "fudging" of the strict financial and budgetary criteria for monetary union laid down in the EU's 1991 Maastricht treaty.
"It's absolutely killing for public confidence in my country. Because people want to maintain their strong currency.

"They want to have it replaced by something else only if they are sure that it will be as stable and as strong as the currency they had. And they have doubts and they don't trust the political establishment that they will handle this fairly," Jochimsen told BBC 2's Newsnight programme.
The BBC released a summary in English of his remarks prior to broadcast.
Jochimsen said five EU states, which he did not name, still harboured hopes of joining the single currency by fudging the the Maastricht criteria.

Interviewed for the same programme, Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet denied France was using creative accounting and said he knew of no one who disputed that France was on course to reduce its budget deficit to less than three percent of national income, as required by the Maastricht treaty.
The European Commission is examining whether the proposed transfer of 37.5 billion francs from France Telecom for the state to cover future pension liabilities was acceptable.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi warned of the consequences if Italy, a founding member of the EU, was not also one of the founding members of the single currency in 1999.
"If there is an almost general entrance (into the single currency), and Italy stays out, the political impact will be terrible," Prodi told Newsnight.
"The feeling of frustration, of weakness of the country, the long-running destiny of the country....this is a deep feeling," he said.
